mcqs.q: Regeneration is the replacement of damaged tissue by:
mcqs.explain: Regeneration replaces damaged tissue with specialized parenchymal cells, restoring the original tissue completely (in cells able to proliferate).

mcqs.q: Repair by scar formation replaces damaged tissue with:
mcqs.explain: Repair replaces tissue with connective tissue, producing fibrosis (a scar); it occurs in cells that cannot proliferate.

mcqs.q: Which are LABILE cells (constantly dividing)?
mcqs.explain: Labile cells (skin, GIT mucosa) divide continuously; stable cells (liver, kidney) divide on demand; permanent cells (nerve, cardiac muscle) do not divide.

mcqs.q: PERMANENT cells, which cannot regenerate, include:
mcqs.explain: Permanent cells (neurons, cardiac muscle) cannot proliferate, so their loss is repaired by scar.

mcqs.q: The four mechanisms of regeneration are migration, differentiation, proliferation and:
mcqs.explain: Regeneration involves cell migration, differentiation, proliferation and matrix formation (collagen, elastin, basement membrane).

mcqs.q: Granulation tissue is composed of:
mcqs.explain: Granulation tissue is fibrosis (collagen laid down by fibroblasts) plus angiogenesis (new blood vessels).

mcqs.q: Fibroblast collagen deposition (fibrosis) is driven mainly by which mediator?
mcqs.explain: Macrophage-derived TGF-β stimulates fibroblasts to lay down collagen (fibrosis); VEGF drives angiogenesis.

mcqs.q: New blood-vessel formation (angiogenesis) in healing is regulated by:
mcqs.explain: Angiogenesis is regulated by VEGF, ECM proteins and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs).

mcqs.q: Healing by PRIMARY intention occurs in a wound that is:
opts: Clean, with opposed edges and little tissue loss
mcqs.explain: Primary intention heals clean surgical wounds with opposed edges and minimal tissue loss, leaving a minimal scar.

mcqs.q: Healing by SECONDARY intention is characterised by:
opts: Separated edges, more granulation tissue, a permanent scar and wound contraction
mcqs.explain: Secondary intention heals large/contaminated wounds with separated edges: abundant granulation tissue, wound contraction and a permanent scar.

mcqs.q: Wound contraction is a feature of:
mcqs.explain: Wound contraction (by myofibroblasts) occurs in secondary-intention healing of large, gaping wounds.

mcqs.q: The FIRST phase of wound healing (within 24 hours) is:
mcqs.explain: Haemostasis is first: platelets aggregate and a clot forms within 24 hours.

mcqs.q: The inflammatory phase of healing (days 1–4) features:
opts: Neutrophil influx, phagocytosis/debridement and release of cytokines
mcqs.explain: The inflammatory phase (days 1–4) involves neutrophil influx, phagocytic debridement and release of cytokines/growth factors.

mcqs.q: The proliferative phase of healing involves:
mcqs.explain: The proliferative phase (around days 4–21) features angiogenesis, collagen deposition, epithelialization and ECM laydown.

mcqs.q: By the end of the maturation/remodeling phase, the scar regains tensile strength of about:
mcqs.explain: During maturation (day 21 – 2 years) collagen is strengthened and the scar reaches ~80% of the original tensile strength.

mcqs.q: Which systemic factor DELAYS wound healing?
opts: Diabetes, steroids, smoking or protein/vitamin deficiency
mcqs.explain: Diabetes, steroids, smoking, old age and deficiencies of protein, vitamin C, vitamin A or zinc all delay healing.

mcqs.q: Vitamin C deficiency impairs healing because it reduces:
mcqs.explain: Vitamin C is needed for collagen hydroxylation/maturation; its deficiency gives weak collagen and fragile vessels (delayed healing).

mcqs.q: How does smoking impair wound healing?
opts: Nicotine causes vasoconstriction and microvascular occlusion
mcqs.explain: Nicotine is a vasoconstrictor that causes microvascular occlusion, reducing perfusion and delaying healing.

mcqs.q: An excessive, raised scar that extends beyond the original wound margins is a:
mcqs.explain: A keloid is excess scar tissue (overgrowth of collagen) extending beyond the wound — a complication of healing.

mcqs.q: Steroids delay healing mainly by:
mcqs.explain: Steroids suppress inflammation by decreasing phagocytosis and chemotaxis, which delays the early stages of healing.

mcqs.q: Interstitial collagen is type ___, while basement-membrane collagen is type ___:
mcqs.explain: Interstitial matrix contains type 1 collagen (with elastin/integrins); the basement membrane contains type 4 collagen.

mcqs.q: A biopsy showing collagen fibres and proliferating blood vessels with minimal inflammation indicates healing at about:
mcqs.explain: Collagen plus proliferating vessels with little inflammation corresponds to the proliferative phase, around 2 weeks after injury.

saqs.q: Differentiate regeneration and repair by scar.
saqs.a: Regeneration replaces tissue with specialized cells → complete restoration. Repair replaces it with connective tissue → fibrosis/scar.

saqs.q: Classify cells by proliferative capacity with examples.
Define granulation tissue and the mediators of its two components.
saqs.a: Fibrosis (collagen by fibroblasts, driven by TGF-β) + angiogenesis (new vessels, driven by VEGF).

saqs.q: Differentiate primary and secondary intention healing.
saqs.a: Primary: clean, opposed edges, little granulation, minimal scar. Secondary: large/contaminated, separated edges, more granulation, permanent scar, wound contraction.

saqs.q: List the four phases of wound healing in order.
List systemic factors that delay wound healing.
saqs.a: ↓ protein, ↓ vitamin C/A, ↓ zinc, steroids, diabetes, smoking, old age.
Infection, dehiscence, contracture, and excess scar (keloid/hypertrophic scar).
